The following three separate orders were issued by the President of India on 29.05.2004 : 
"1. Whereas the office of the Speaker will become vacant immediately before the commencement of the first sitting of the House of the People on the 2nd June, 2004 and the office of the Deputy Speaker is also vacant; 
Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred upon me by clause (1) of article 95 of the Constitution of India, I hereby appoint Shri Somnath Chatterjee, a Member of the House of the People, to perform the duties of the office of the Speaker from the commencement of the said sitting, i.e. the 2nd of June, 2004, and until the commencement of the sitting of the House of the People on 4th of June, 2004.

FELICITATIONS TO THE SPEAKER 
Title: Felicitations to Shri Somnath Chatterjee on his election as the Speaker of Fourteenth Lok Sabha. 

THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. Speaker Sir, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru once said that in affairs of the State, one should be full of sentiments but never be sentimental. You will forgive me for being somewhat sentimental on this occasion. 
Some 50 years ago, when I graduated from my college, your illustrious father presided over the Convocation where I got the degree and today, Sir, when I am going to assume a new office, you are in this illustrious Chair as our guide, friend and philosopher. 
Sir, it is a privilege for me to congratulate you and felicitate you on behalf of our Party and on my own behalf on your unanimous election as Speaker of this august House. 
You, Mr. Speaker Sir, have been an illustrious Member of this august House for over three decades. The Members of the House, quite correctly, showed their appreciation of your vast contribution to the proceedings by conferring on you the Outstanding Parliamentarian Award some years ago, and now by unanimously electing you to this august House as Speaker. 
Sir, your life and work as a parliamentarian have been a source of tremendous inspiration for many of us. Like you, I have always believed that politics has to be used as an instrument of social change. To realise this vision, heavy responsibility rests on the Members of this august House and Sir, in you, we have a wise shepherd to guide us. The Members of my party and of the United Progressive Alliance will be with you in your endeavour to improve the quality of debate, discussion and the content of the legislative outcome of our proceedings. 
Mr. Speaker Sir, this House reflects the diversity of our vast and plural nation and debates here do reflect the diversity of opinion in our democracy. However, the manner in which our proceedings are conducted and the effectiveness with which we use the time at our disposal to redeem our pledge to the people determine how effectively we can contribute to the holy endeavour of nation building. 
Sir, given your wisdom, given your commitment to our Republic and its ideals, I am sure you will conduct the proceedings of the House in the highest traditions of our great democracy. I assure you, Sir, of my fullest cooperation and indeed of our Alliance and of our Party. I sincerely wish you well, Mr. Speaker Sir, in your responsibility to make the best use of the time at our disposal so that we can deliver on our promises, lighting a lamp in the lives of our people, 
particularly, the deprived sections of our community. We are committed to taking our nation forward as a modern, progressive, open, secular and liberal democracy and a just society. 
Under your guidance, Sir, this House will not disappoint the nation. I sincerely hope that our deliberations will be characterised by reason, compassion and a deep commitment to both efficiency and equity in the processes of governance. We have, Sir, to recapture the high noon of idealism, which inspired our freedom struggle. This idealism is best captured by Rabindra Nath Tagore’s famous Poem, and I shall conclude with the prayer that under your distinguished guidance, in our deliberations we live up to the high ideals embodied in that poem:  "Where the mind is without fear, and the head is held high; 
Where knowledge is free; 
Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls; 
Where words come out from the depth of truth; 
Where tireless striving stretches its arms towards perfection; 
Where the clear stream of reason has not lost its way into the dreary desert sand of dead habit; 
Where the mind is led forward by thee into ever-widening thought and action— 
Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake."  I congratulate you, Sir, once again on this occasion. 

THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): Mr. Speaker Sir, I join the Prime Minister in congratulating you on your unanimous election to this august office. 
Sir, the first Lok Sabha Sabha, under the new Constitution, had the privilege of having your illustrious father as a Member of this House. Since 1971, you are Member of this House and you have contributed very effectively in the deliberations of the House. Your recognition as one of the outstanding parliamentarians, keeping in view your contributions, speaks the quality of your mind and heart. 
Sir, today you have joined the line of illustrious predecessors starting from Shri Vithalbhai Patel to Shri Mavalankar and many others who have not only raised the status of this office but also upheld the dignity, prestige and honour of our Sovereign, Democratic Republic. 
Sir, this high-domed hall has witnessed many histories. Even long before Independence our legislatures asserted for autonomy. If I remember correctly, in 1924, a question arose about the independence of the Central Legislative Assembly as it was called then, and then under the inspiration of the then Speaker, Shri Motilal Nehru, as leader of the Swaraj Party, moved the Motion that let the establishment of the Central Legislative Assembly be placed under the control of the Speaker, not under the control of the Executive. And since then, we have maintained this tradition. As the hon. Prime Minister has very correctly pointed out, you would be the custodian, you will guide us; and we do hope that with your experience and vast knowledge of the Constitution, you will uphold the right of this House of having control on money and finance. Not a single paisa can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without the approval of this House. Not a single penny can be spent. But, unfortunately, in our preoccupation on other matters, this aspect has been lost sight of. I remember when our budgetary transactions did not cross four figure, when our First Five Year Plan was in the order of Rs.2000 crore, Parliament used to, especially Lok Sabha Sabha, spend more than two-thirds of its time on money and finance. And when the budgetary transaction has crossed more than four lakh crores of rupees, hardly we have any time to ponder, to scrutinise it. I do hope that under your guidance, Parliament will assert its authority over Executive and surely the debate and deliberations of this House will inspire the new generation which has come. 
Thank you Mr. Speaker Sir and once again my heartiest congratulations.

SHRIMATI SONIA GANDHI (RAEBARELI) : Let me add a few words of greetings to the newly elected hon. Speaker Shri Somnath Chatterjee. 
Somnathji’s Parliamentary skills have been widely recognised and justly applauded. His legal acumen has been much appreciated and, if I may say so, also rewarded. But today I also greet another Somnathji, a much respected colleague whose counsel my party and I have sought and valued. 
In honouring him this morning, we are reaffirming our deep and abiding faith in the best tradition of India in her diversity and in her plurality. The election that brought all of us to this House has one overriding message and that message is that the people of our country have rejected the politics of divisiveness. In many ways, the multi-faceted personality of Somnathji reflects that verdict. He is a thoroughly modern man steeped in tradition, a person rooted in ideology but wedded to pragmatism. He combines an unwavering commitment to certain basic principles with a rare ability to reach across the political divide and make good friends. Somnathji has an unflinching commitment to the liberal values of Indian culture, yet is always open to debate and discussion with those who do not share his passion for those values. In honouring him today, we honour one who has graced this House for over three decades with his erudition, his wit, his vast learning and experience. 
Somnathji has elevated the proceedings and deliberations of this august House. As a Speaker, he would, I suppose, have to speak less and listen more. We would miss his debates but our political life would be, I am sure, immeasurably enhanced with him in his new role. 
On my behalf and on behalf of my party, I wish to assure him of our fullest co-operation at all times, both in the House and in his Chambers where much of Parliamentary business gets transacted. We know that he would be fair. We know that his rulings would always be reasoned and measured and his decisions would always be taken in the national interest. 
Mr. Speaker, Sir, this marks a new innings in your long and distinguished career. We wish you all the very best. 
MR. SPEAKER: Thank you.

SHRI BASUDEB ACHARIA (BANKURA): Mr. Speaker, Sir, on my behalf and on behalf of the entire Left Group, I congratulate and felicitate you on your assumption of this high office. 
I have not seen during my 24 years in this House that a Speaker was elected with an overwhelming support from the entire House. For the first time I have 
seen such an overwhelming support that you have received from all sections of this House. 
We are delighted to see that such an eminent parliamentarian like you, with a very long experience of Parliament, has now been elevated to this high position. It has been done unanimously which demonstrates that the Indian democracy has matured, which is now reflected in the recent Lok Sabha Sabha elections. 
Sir, we are doubly happy and proud on this solemn occasion because you are the leader of my Party and one of the top leaders of Left Front. We have seen how you had sincerely tried to unite, when you were in the Opposition, all the Parties belonging to the Opposition and the secular forces of our country. You took the lead to unite all the political parties believing in secularism. 
Sir, it goes without saying that you will be very successful in running the House and listening to and giving opportunities to all sections of the House, not only the leader of the CPI(M) but to all, not only to leaders but to all Members of the House. Sir, this time majority of the Members are new. Most of them have come for the first time to this House. We have seen also how you always tried to uphold the dignity and decorum of this House. With your elevation to the post of Speaker, we sincerely hope that the decorum and dignity of the House which has deteriorated in the last several years, can be lifted under your guidance and under your leadership. 
Sir, you have excellent ingredients in your personality to present to our countrymen and the outside world also that the people’s representatives have been functioning in most responsible and befitting manner which is now necessary. What we have seen in the past is that there are burning issues and problems which the people of our country are facing. We have poverty, we have unemployment, and we have starvation deaths in our country. We, the representatives of the people, should get the opportunity to ventilate the grievances. … (Interruptions) 
MR. SPEAKER : It seems I will have to start with controlling the leader of the CPI(M) first. Please try to conclude. 
SHRI BASUDEB ACHARIA : Sir, with your elevation to this high office, we have lost a great speaker and a leader outside. I wish you all success and I assure you all cooperation, fullest cooperation from the entire Left Group. Thank you. 
MR. SPEAKER : Thank you very much.

SHRI C. KUPPUSAMI (MADRAS NORTH): Hon. Speaker, Sir, Vanakkam. 
On behalf of respected Dr. Kalaignar M. Karunanidhi, the President of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, and the rank and file of the DMK Party, I express our felicitations and unstinted support to you, Sir, as you embark upon a new chapter in your distinguished political career as Hon. Speaker of the Fourteenth Lok Sabha. 
Our founding fathers decided to adopt the parliamentary system of governance for our great nation. The Lok Sabha along with the Rajya Sabha occupies the pivotal position in our democratic set up. As democratically elected representatives, the Parliament provides us the sacred opportunity to highlight and find solutions for the problems of the common people, the peasants, the working class and the vulnerable sections of the society. 
Since 1971, Sir, you have created a chequered history in the Indian Parliament during your long innings. In recognition of your immense and invaluable contributions towards strengthening of our parliamentary set up in its every aspect, you have been honoured with the Outstanding Parliamentarian Award in 1997. 
Mr. Speaker, Sir, this august House and this great country knows very well that you have been a speaker for the downtrodden, the poorest of the poor, the exploited ones, the peasants, labourers and workers and all the toiling masses of the Indian society, which reverberated in this great House for many decades. In the real sense, you are the torch-bearer of the downtrodden. 
With great pleasure and pride, I would like to once again compliment you, Sir, on your taking over as the hon. Speaker of the Fourteenth Lok Sabha. 
Thank you very much.

SHRI BRAJA KISHORE TRIPATHY (PURI): Mr. Speaker, Sir, it is a great pleasure and privilege on my part to extend to you my warm welcome. On this auspicious occasion. I felicitate you on my own behalf and on behalf of my party, Biju Janata Dal. 
Sir, in the past, you have been rightly rewarded as the Best Parliamentarian. You are not only one of the Best Parliamentarian of the time, you are also a leading legal luminary of the country. You have the expertise in interpreting the constitutional laws. In this interpretation, you have earned vast experience. You have vast experience in Parliament as a parliamentarian and also as a legal expert. You have the experience of practising law in the Apex Court, the Supreme Court of India. So, we have that advantage. 
On the one hand you have the advantage of making laws in this apex Panchayat, in this Parliament; and on the other hand you have the experience of implementing the decisions and interpreting the same laws in the Supreme Court, the Apex Court. So, we, the Members, have the advantage of getting your judicious advice and your guidance in this august House. 
Sir, I am extremely happy that you have been chosen as the Speaker of this House rightly and unanimously. I hope, you will maintain the high dignity and decorum of this House and you will also be able to strengthen the parliamentary democracy not only in our country but also the world over. We are sure, you will give a leading light to strengthen the parliamentary democracy. 
Sir, I hope, your parliamentary career with vast experience and your entire devotion for the human lives and the common man will definitely help this august House to extend the best for the countrymen. 
I wish you again the very best from all of us for all the time. Thank you. 
MR. SPEAKER: Thank you. 

SHRI P.K. VASUDEVAN NAIR (THIRUVANANTHAPURAM): Mr. Speaker, Sir, on behalf of my party and myself, I have great pleasure in extending to you our hearty congratulations on this very happy occasion. 
Sir, a person like you was normally not expected to occupy such a constitutional Chair in the old days. The fact that you are sitting in that Chair shows that the times are changing, that our political scenario is going through a big change. And, I hope, much bigger changes are coming. This is an indication, of that according to me. 
Sir, this election has shown that millions of toiling people in this counry are in utter despair and they are feeling frustrated. After more than half a century of freedom, it is a pity that these millions of people are feeling like that. So, let us take note of that in all seriousness. I am happy that a person who can understand the aspirations of these toiling millions is occupying this Chair at this point of time. 
Sir, I would like to say one more thing. Of course, there is no need to advise you on your functioning. Even before occupying that Chair, you have said that you would be very considerate to the Opposition. You said that you would even like to pamper the Opposition. 
Our legislatures are under criticism by the people of the country these days. Very unfortunate things are taking place in our legislatures. We used to be blamed, but it is not the question now. I have felt that there was a tendency to steamroll the Opposition – whichever Party it may be. But your idea, that the Opposition should be given consideration or a little more partiality, is a very good step in restoring the noble practices of our parliamentary democracy. I wish you all success.

PROF. M.RAMADASS (PONDICHERRY): Hon. Speaker, Sir, the Pattali Makkal Katchi of Tamil Nadu, the party I represent, deems it a pride and pleasure to congratulate you on this historic occasion of your elevation as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Our Founder-President Dr. Ramdass Aiya, one of the architects of UPA’s resounding victory in Tamil Nadu and the labour community of Tamil Nadu, whose aspirations the PMK represents in this august House, join me in offering their choicest felicitations to you on your elevation. 
Sir, I should also compliment Shrimati Sonia Gandhi who has been instrumental for a consensual approach to elect you unanimously as the Speaker with overwhelming support of all shades of opinion in this House. This is a rare gesture of not only the Hon. Members who are present here to elect you unanimously and through them the people of India have also chosen you as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Even when the first Speaker of Lok Sabha Shri G.V.Mavalankar was elected in 1952, there was a contest. But today, a consensual approach initiated by Shrimati Sonia Gandhi in your election augurs well for this Lok Sabha and I hope that this is the beginning of a healthy political tradition that we are going to unveil in the near future. For setting this highest tradition of democracy, the Pattali Makkal Katchi compliments Shrimati Sonia Gandhi in an abundant measure. 
Sir, as the architect of your unanimous election, I humbly feel that Shrimati Sonia Gandhi seems to have followed two of the major recommendations of the Page Committee which was constituted in 1967 to suggest some of the conventions on the election of the Speaker. Two of the recommendations of the Page Committee were : (1) the party in power should evolve a consensus on who should be the Speaker. In this case, the party (Congress) in power had been trying to evolve this consensus over the last fortnight and it has been successful. The second condition was that the person nominated should be of considerable seniority and should enjoy a prestige similar to that of the Leader of the House. Sir, in your election, these two conditions are more than satisfied and I hope that the people of this country should feel happy for choosing you as the Speaker of the House unanimously. We hope that with your rich experience in this House, you would be able to conduct the proceedings of the House in a dignified and decorous way. 
Sir, you have said two to three days back in the Press that you would try to pamper the Opposition by giving them enough opportunity and the same should be extended to parties like us, who are not numerically strong enough but who have a lot of ideas to contribute to the larger issues that would be coming up before the Lok Sabha. Therefore, I would appeal to you Sir that you should be able to give us opportunities for offering our views. Sir, I come from Pondichery the land of Aurobindo and Bharatidasan – the people of that land also join me in offering the choicest felicitations to you. I hope that during your tenure as the Speaker you would be able to see Parliament as an instrument of change. Our hon. Prime Minister in his felicitation address said that politics is going to be the instrument of change. This politics has to be translated into a reality through the businesses that we are going to transact in this Lok Sabha. Therefore, you are the custodian of the people of this country. One hundred and three crore people of this country expects much deliverance from you. I hope, with the good wishes of the people of India you would be able to render your services more effectively and efficaciously. 

THE MINISTER WITHOUT PORTFOLIO (SHRI K. CHANDRA SHEKHAR RAO): Sir, I congratulate you profusely on your unanimous election as the Speaker of this august House. In fact, this House is privileged to have a veteran parliamentarian like you as the Speaker. You are one of the best parliamentarians of the country who is held in high esteem by everyone in this country. Your vast and rich experience will be a great source of inspiration to the old and newly elected Members of this House and to the aspiring masses of the country. 
I wish you all success and all the best on my own behalf and on behalf of the Members of my party, Telengana Rashtriya Samiti. 
Sir, I also assure you our fullest co-operation in maintaining the dignity and decorum of this House. 

DR. MANDA JAGANNATH (NAGARKURNOOL): Sir, on behalf of the Telugu Desam Parliamentary Party and on my own behalf, I congratulate you heartily for unanimously getting elected as the Speaker of the Fourteenth Lok Sabha. 
Sir, you have created history by being the first communist leader to occupy the coveted post of the Lok Sabha Speaker. It is really a fitting tribute to your honour as you have been elected for a record ten terms to Lok Sabha mostly from the famous Bolpur constituency known for the Vishwa Bharati University. 
I also welcome you as a senior Member who has enjoyed respect and prestige similar to that of the Leader of the House. You are a powerful speaker known for your wit and sarcasm and a recipient of the Outstanding Parliamentarian Award in 1996. Sir, your elevation will be a loss to us in the sense that we will miss your oratory in the House but we will get benefited by your guidance in running the House properly. I do not know how many of us are aware that you are a renowned Barrister-at-Law and actively associated with various educational, cultural and professional institutions like the Indian Law Institute and the International Law Association. Sir, you are also connected with a number of trade unions which are helping the working class. 
You have been in Parliament for more than three decades and have earned a reputation for doing your homework meticulously and maintaining civility and decorum in dealing with political opponents. Your career as the Speaker will call for tactfulness, patience and above all an unwavering impartiality. 
On behalf of myself and on behalf of the Telugu Desam Parliamentary Party, I extend my assurance for co-operation in running the business of the House smoothly. I expect that, after sitting in the Opposition benches for decades, you would take the liberty of giving more time to Opposition Members to express their views on various matters under discussion in the House. 
Finally, besides felicitating you as the Speaker, I extend our best wishes once again on my own behalf and on behalf of Telugu Desam Parliamentary Party.

SHRI P.A. SANGMA (TURA): Mr. Speaker, Sir, seven years ago, on the 19th of March, 1997, I had the privilege of conferring on you the ‘Outstanding Parliamentarian Award’ for 1996. On that occasion this is what I said about you. I quote:  "Internally I have always assigned to Shri Somnath Chatterjee the status of my guru. "  Sir, today after this unanimous election to the post of Speaker, you have indeed become the maha guru for everyone of us here. 
I had the privilege of travelling with you both in India as well as abroad. On more than one occasion, I have told my friends that being with Shri Somnath Chatterjee itself is an experience, knowledge and an intellectual elevation. I do not forget the important role you have played on behalf of Indian Parliament in Beijing in the IPO Conference where you have been unopposedly chosen as the rapporteur of the Conference. 
Today, I feel really very happy to see my Guru sitting in the Chair. I wish you all the best. I wish you a very successful tenure and I congratulate you from the core of my heart. 
May God bless you, Sir! 
MR. SPEAKER: Thank you very much. Next, Shri Bir Singh Mahato.

So, on behalf of my Party and the Left Group, I congratulate you. Thank you, Sir.

DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMAH (LAKHIMPUR): Hon. Speaker, Sir, on behalf my party, Asom Gana Parishad, my President, Shri Brindavan Goswami and on my own behalf, I congratulate you and also felicitate you on your unanimous election to the office of the Speaker of this august House. 
Sir, I will be failing in my duty if I do not express the special feelings of the people of Assam. Since you were born in Tezpur of Assam, I take the privilege of conveying the special greetings to you on behalf of the people of Assam. 
MR. SPEAKER: Thank you. 
DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMAH : Sir, considering your vast experience and long association with parliamentary procedures, I am confident that the House would be greatly benefited and would be able to deliver the goods to the nation. And also your being a member of the legal profession, I hope your neutrality, judicious decisions and logical conclusions will satisfy all sections and all political entities of this House, especially the smaller parties by getting adequate opportunities to express their viewpoints. 
Sir, I am not very old to parliamentary proceedings in Lok Sabha. I have the experience of only 18 months in the 11th Lok Sabha. With that experience, I feel that we waste more time in accusations and counter-accusations made by bigger parties. There is hardly any serious debate on serious issues through which we can deliver the goods to the nation. I hope, with your ability and statesmanship, you will be able to curtail the unproductive deliberations in the House. 
Lastly, I assure you full cooperation and wish you a successful tenure on behalf of my party and on my own behalf. Thank you very much. 
MR. SPEAKER: Hon. Members, I hope you will spare little time to the Speaker to respond. We are now nearing one o’clock. But I will call some other hon. Members who have been kind enough to send in their names with a request. I am sure they will appreciate that brevity is a virtue.

SHRI H.D. DEVE GOWDA (HASSAN): Mr. Speaker Sir, it is one of the happiest occasions for me to extend my heart-felt congratulations and felicitations. 
Sir, I have always been inspired by you, as a Member of this House, since I entered this apex institution in 1991. Today, you have been elected unanimously. That shows the love and affection you have earned in the last three decades as a Member of this House. 
Sitting in the Opposition, you have inspired the entire House by your eloquent speeches. You have never spared anybody while exposing the failures of the Government -- whether this Government or that Government -- whenever you felt. I am very happy that today you have accepted this high office and you are the custodian of this apex institution. 
Sir, with much pain if I say a word, the erosion of parliamentary democratic system in this country is painful to all of us. Within a short duration of about seven to eight years, I witnessed how we are all responsible for the erosion of all values in public life. The people talk with worry and they give such a scant respect to the political parties and to the political system, for which we are responsible. I do not want to blame anybody in this country, but we all contributed to such a situation. 
May I humbly request the leaders of the ruling party as well as the Opposition to extend their full co-operation, their total co-operation, their absolute co-operation to restore the values, to restore the dignity, decorum and decency of this House? Unless that is done, I am sorry, Sir, we are not going to achieve anything. At this stage, it is not the issue to discuss our political ideologies and commitments. I know the commitment of the Left for the working class and also for the poorer sections of the people. I am with you on this. I do not want to elaborate on this issue. 
But today your responsibility is more. We are all concerned to make this House functional to deliberate on the issues. Whether it is the issue of minorities or the oppressed or the suppressed or the working class or the organised or the unorganised, that is left to the entire House, especially to the ruling party which has to take more responsibility on these issues. 
Sir, in my political career of 44 years -–but most of my career was spent in the State Legislature—only once I broke the tradition. You were all here. Late Indrajit Gupta was here. Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee, one of the senior-most parliamentarians, was sitting this side. Sir, on the issue of farmers, on the issue of the World Bank’s conditions and conditionalities, I opposed it and I went to the Well breaking all the norms in my political career. Remember these words. I only request the ruling party and the entire House to deliberate and spend the valuable time for the purpose of solving the problem of suffering masses. 
With these words, from the core of my heart, I would like to extend my heartfelt congratulations and felicitations to your elevation to the highest office. I convey my good wishes on behalf of myself and on behalf of my Party. 
Thank you very much. 
MR. SPEAKER: Thank you.

SHRI ASADUDDIN OWAISI (HYDERABAD): Mr. Speaker, Sir, I congratulate you on your unanimous election as the Speaker of this august House. 
With your long experience in the field of Parliamentary democracy, I am sure, you would get the support of each and every Member of this House. At the same time, I would like to say that the new Members are most fortunate to have you as the Speaker of this august House. 
It has been already expressed by various Members that there are many Members who represent smaller parties. I am one of them. I represent the historic city of Hyderabad. I am sure, with you in the Chair, the Lok Sabha would really shine and India would really shine through lively debates in this august House. 
I know that you had been called to the bar from Middle Temple. The barrister in you would not forget another barrister in me who has been called from Lincoln’s Inn. I request you that smaller parties may be given more time and opportunities to raise issues concerning the common man and in particular issues relating to the minorities.

SHRI P.C. THOMAS (MUVATTUPUZHA): I take this opportunity to congratulate you on your elevation as the Speaker of this august House.

I come from Kerala and I come from a constituency where pineapples are grown. It is not spicy but it is very sweet. I would like to offer a sweet pineapple to you just now but I am sorry I would not be able to bring it here. I just want to highlight the issues of farmers. Pineapples, coconut and rubber are farm products of Kerala that are a little different from farm products which are grown elsewhere. So, we may be given opportunities to raise the issues of those farmers. I am sure that you are a person who has got common sense which is very uncommon nowadays. I would also like to say that all my colleagues from Kerala are sitting on the other side. So, sometimes, you may have to look at me just to give me a little more chance to say a word of dissent. 
I take this opportunity to congratulate you once again and also to pray to God that the experience you have would be of great help to all the Members of this House and to all the sections of this House.

MR. SPEAKER: Hon. Members, I am extremely thankful to you for unanimously electing me to the high office of the Speaker of this august House. I do not have words adequately to express my feelings for the great honour bestowed on me and I accept the same with all humility and gratitude. I am overwhelmed by the generous sentiments expressed for me by all sections of the House. 
Today I cannot help remembering the day when I first entered this great Chamber in the year 1971 as a new Member and I must confess that I was overawed in the presence of giants and luminaries who added great lustre to the proceedings of the House. As a back bencher, I had the opportunity to listen to some of the great orations inside the House which inspired me to be worthy of the confidence reposed by the people by electing me to the House. I cannot also forget witnessing from the Visitors’ Gallery on occasions the proceedings in the House when my father, late Shri N.C. Chatterjee, was one of the Members. I had the great privilege of hearing some of the most inspiring interventions by, amongst others, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel, Pandit Pant, Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee, Shri N. C. Chatterjee, Prof. Hiren Mukherjee, Shri Nath Pai and many others. Please excuse me for the nostalgic feeling that I have on this occasion. 
I am also grateful to the hon. Prime Minister for his kind reference to my father. I find his award of degree to him was well justified and he has more than proved his merit, and today I must congratulate him once again for occupying this position of high honour. 
Hon. Members, the Fourteenth Lok Sabha has got the people’s mandate to usher in a new era. This is a unique responsibility bestowed on this august House. Our country has made progress in various fields since Independence. However, a lot more needs to be done for the benefit of the common people. We have to ensure that the creative potential and energies of our people are harnessed for fulfilling the hopes and aspirations of various sections of our society, particularly the deprived and the dispossessed, by providing a developing, pro-people and secular administration. 
Lok Sabha is the highest elected body in the largest parliamentary democracy in the world and occupies the pivotal position in our political system. Our founding fathers, after considerable deliberations, decided to adopt the parliamentary system of governance with the Lok Sabha elected on adult franchise and the Council of Ministers responsible to the same. The people of India participate in the parliamentary process through their representatives in Lok Sabha. Members of Parliament who are elected on the basis of their pledge contained in their manifestoes are expected to articulate the urges and aspirations of the people, to discuss problems and issues facing the nation and to deliberate upon the formulation of national policies and programmes with a view to finding solutions to them. The very postulate of parliamentary democracy as is enshrined in our Constitution is the collective responsibility of Central Council of Ministers to the House of People. For every action of the Government it is liable to answer in this House. 
This House represents all sections of our people with their very socio-cultural identities, ethos and genius, differences of ideas, interests, approaches and objectives as they are bound to arise during the deliberations in the House. As a strong integrating force in the country, this House, which is the people’s institution in the true sense of the term is called upon to resolve the various socio-political and economic problems faced by the people. 
Even after more than five decades of Independence, in course of which we have celebrated the Golden Jubilee of our Parliament, a very substantial number of our people still face awesome problems and do not enjoy even the minimum rights which the Constitution, our organic law contemplates for them. Abysmal poverty, illiteracy, high child mortality, absence of adequate healthcare, lack of job opportunities, non-availability of pure drinking water in many areas, amongst others, are the problems which still haunt the common people and resulted in effective denial of the constitutional and indeed the basic human rights to our people. 
The common people of our country, particularly the toiling sections, the workers, the peasants and the farmers, the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, the women and the minorities have not been able to fulfil their minimum needs. The condition of the working class in the country is still extremely uncertain with mounting unemployment figures. In such circumstances, I humbly feel that it is the bounden duty of us all, as Members of Parliament, to play a very active, responsible and effective role to meet the aspirations of the people. 
The Parliament is constituted by the people. It has to deliberate upon and deal with the problems of the people and ultimately find their solutions for the people. 
The Rules of business and procedure in Lok Sabha have been framed for the orderly conduct of its business and several avenues for obtaining redressal of the people’s grievances have also been provided in the rules. My appeal to all the hon. Members is to utilise these rules in a proper manner so that they can play an effective role as Members of this august House. 
Nowadays considerable criticism is being faced by the Members of Parliament about their failure to maintain decorum and dignity in the House. The behaviour and conduct of some legislators have become subject of justified criticism and in some cases even of ridicule. Unfortunately, there is developing more and more an attitude of confrontation than cooperation in our political life which finds its reflection in the House. We should resolve to change this perception in the minds of the people by our own conduct, both inside and outside the House. 
Hon. Members, I am fully conscious of the responsibility bestowed on me as the Speaker of this august House. The willing co-operation you have promised today on the floor of the House gives the strength to shoulder the great responsibility and prove myself worthy of the trust you have reposed in me. Conscious as I am of the responsibility that has been entrusted, I can assure you that I shall always endeavour to conduct the business of this House in keeping with the lofty ideals and noble goals enshrined in our great Constitution and in the Rules of Procedure and in tune with the highest parliamentary traditions. 
I am fully aware that as the Speaker, my conduct and behaviour will always be under close scrutiny. Maintaining the high standards laid down by the distinguished predecessors starting from Shri Vithalbhai Patel, Shri G.V. Mavalankar up to Shri Manohar Joshi, I shall spare no effort to uphold and, if possible, further enhance the dignity and prestige of this high constitutional office in regulating the proceedings of this House and addressing the concerns of its Members. 
I shall discharge my functions entrusted to this office more as a duty rather than as an authority. The non-party character of the office of the Speaker in our parliamentary polity places on me a special obligation to be totally non-partisan and judicious while regulating the proceedings of the House. So long as I occupy this exalted Chair, I assure you that I shall always strive to protect to the best of my ability the rights and privileges of the House and of its Members irrespective of their political affiliations. 
Hon. Members, I can assure you that to me, all the hon. Members are of the same status and are entitled to the same facilities, irrespective of the party to which one may belong, and will be entitled to the same opportunity. The only status that I recognise is that all of you are elected and hon. Members of this great institution. 
Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru had observed at a Seminar on Parliamentary Democracy held on 6th December, 1957 that:  "Deliberately and after long argument, we in India adopted a Constitution based on parliamentary Government. We praise the parliamentary form of Government because it is a peaceful method of dealing with problems. It is a method of agreement, discussion, decision and accepting the decision even though one may or may not agree with it. However, a minority in a parliamentary Government has a very important part to play. Naturally, the majority by the mere fact that it is majority must have its way. "  Parliament should function through debate, discussion and consensus and it can only do so if the deliberations are marked by a sense of commitment to the cause of the people and the atmosphere in the House is kept free from bitterness and acrimony. Unless the rules, regulations and well-established parliamentary conventions are respected by each and every Member and unless the Members exhibit mutual accommodation and respect whenever there are differing points of view, our parliamentary democracy will remain imperfect. The Treasury Benches and the Opposition have equal responsibilities in ensuring good governance in the country. While discharging their parliamentary responsibilities, both sides are expected to be accommodating and forbearing to each other, particularly when contentious issues are debated on the floor of the House. 
A Member of Parliament occupies a very high place in the eyes of the people. The effectiveness of the functioning of this House would depend to a great extent on how scrupulously we, the Members follow various rules and guidelines which are a prerequisite for the orderly transaction of parliamentary business. Here, I need hardly emphasise that the observance of discipline and decorum on the part of the Members is an essential pre-condition for the smooth and efficient functioning of the House. Besides the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business, there exist numerous customs and conventions, rules of parliamentary etiquette and unrecorded traditions, which have to be observed by every Member in the interest of parliamentary decorum. One need hardly emphasise that it is the quality of our behaviour and the substance of our deliberations that will decide whether we are able to enhance the prestige of this august House and promote faith in our parliamentary institution. 
With many young faces making their debut in the Lok Sabha in the just concluded General Elections, this House has the benefit of utilising a pool of constructive energies together with experience of the senior Members in responding to the issues concerning the hopes and aspirations of the common masses. 
I hope every newly elected Member will function with commitment and learn and follow the rules of the game and make valuable contributions to the proceedings of the House. May I suggest the newcomers may get themselves conversant with the established parliamentary traditions and conventions and learn to make full use of all their valuable procedural devices so that they may contribute effectively towards redressal of the people’s grievances. 
The role of the media in providing an effective interface between the people and the Parliament cannot be overemphasised. I am fully confident that a responsible and adequate coverage of the proceedings of the House by the media will go a long way in projecting the right image of the supreme national forum. I seek a meaningful cooperation from the media. 
I am grateful to the hon. Members for their warm expressions about me and for assuring me their unstinted cooperation. I express my grateful thanks to the hon. Prime Minister; hon. Leader of the House; Shrimati Sonia Gandhi; Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee; hon. Leader of Opposition, Shri L. K. Advani; Leaders of various Parties; and other distinguished friends for the warm sentiments they have expressed about me. To run the House successfully, I look forward to your cooperation. On my part let me assure you once again that I shall endeavour my best to justify the trust that you have reposed in me and meet your expectations. 
Let us all join our hands in heralding a new era of peace, progress and prosperity for our country through the discharge of our duty as the chosen representatives of the people. I earnestly seek your kind cooperation and help in the discharge of my onerous duty. 
As a Leftist, as one belonging to the Left Party, friends on my left may be rest assured that I have a natural leaning towards the left. Let us resolve that we shall perform the task assigned to us to the best of our ability and with sincerity. We should ask ourselves when the House rises for the day every evening as to what we have done during the day for the country and for the people and whether we have justified the people’s faith in sending us here. Nothing will give us more satisfaction than the feeling that we have tried and done our best. 
Thank you very much. 
Friends, there are three hon. Members who have not yet been able to take oath, and out of those three hon. Members, one is very unwell. May I give them the opportunity to take the oath? Yes Secretary-General, please call the names.
